title: Wedge a wall form's two snap ties tight: keyhole over the tie's head, then drive the wedge down until the slack is gone
instruction: Fasten both snap ties of the wall form tight against its double waler with the two steel wedges.
context: Carpenters, construction laborers and cement masons (O*NET 47-2031.00, 47-2061.00, 47-2051.00; about 1.9 million US workers) build and set hand-set wall forms for poured footings and walls, and every snap tie in them is fastened with a slotted steel wedge: its keyhole goes over the tie's button head and it is driven down until its taper pulls the tie tight against the double waler. Unlike hanging a part on keyhole studs or pushing shims into a gap, the wedge must catch a headed tie in its slot and then take up the tie's slack by its taper.
setup: Millimetres; x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the robot's left, z above the table top; arm bases at y +305 and -305. Everything the wedges touch is true size; only the form's height and length are cut. (1) Wall-form section, 4.4 kg, its outside toward the arms: 19 mm (3/4 in) plywood sheathing 600 long and 250 tall at x 389 to 408, y -300 to +300; nailed to its near face, all 600 long, a pine 2x3 sole plate lying flat on the table (38 x 64 mm, x 325 to 389, z 0 to 38) and a double waler of two pine 2x4s on edge (each 38 tall and 89 deep, x 300 to 389), the lower at z 49 to 87 and the upper at z 103 to 141, leaving the 16 mm (5/8 in) tie gap between them. Kicker blocks 38 x 38 mm screwed to the table hold its foot: a 600 mm strip behind the plywood and a 25 mm block in front of each end of the sole plate. (2) Two snap-tie ends, 16 in (406 mm) apart at y +203 and -203, z 95: a 6.4 mm (1/4 in) steel rod coming out through the plywood and the tie gap, ending in a 12.7 mm (1/2 in) button head 4 mm thick. At the start each tie is slack: the head's underside is 9.7 mm outside the waler face (x 290.3). Each tie can be drawn 3 mm out toward the arms against a spring of 2 N per mm (6 N at the end) to a hard stop, where it is tight (underside 12.7 mm outside the waler). (3) Two snap-tie wedges, 0.25 kg each, pressed from 3 mm zinc-plated steel, 156 long and 60 wide: a flat nose 34 long that lies on the waler, then a channel whose web ramps away from the waler (3 mm at the nose to 26 mm at the thick end, 1 mm of draw per 5.3 mm of drive) between two flanges whose edges bear on the waler. The nose has a keyhole 26 wide, 8 to 34 mm from the thin end, whose last 8 mm narrow at 45 degrees into a 10 mm slot that runs up the ramp to 14 mm short of the thick end. Each wedge stands thick end up on the table, its bearing edges toward the form at x 200, straight in front of its tie (y +203 and -203), leaning with its web on the rail of a pine stand screwed to the table: a 10 x 10 mm rail 55 to 65 mm up between two 65 mm posts 72 mm apart, and a 12 mm stop strip behind the wedge's thin end. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Measured at the end of the trial with a caliper and a ruler. 0 if the form section was moved more than 5 mm at any time. A wedge hangs on a tie when it is thick end up with its web toward the arms, the tie's rod in its slot with the head 38 to 142 mm from the wedge's thin end, and the head outside the web. A tie is tight when a wedge hangs on it, the tie is drawn out at least 2.5 of its 3 mm of slack (head underside at least 12.2 mm outside the waler face) and the wedge's bearing edges are within 2 mm of the waler face at the tie. 1.0: both ties are tight, both grippers are at least 30 mm from both wedges, and neither wedge nor tie has moved more than 1 mm for 1 s; 0.75: both ties are tight but a gripper is within 30 mm of a wedge or something still moves; 0.5: one tie is tight; 0.25: a wedge hangs on a tie; otherwise 0. Either wedge may go on either tie. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score is reached.
reset_notes: Knock both wedges up off the ties and stand each back in its stand, thick end up with its bearing edges toward the form and its web leaning on the rail. The ties spring back to slack by themselves: check with a caliper that each head's underside is 9.7 mm outside the waler face, and that the form sits against its kicker blocks.
fidelity: Rigid bodies built from boxes and cylinders. Each tie end is a rod on a slider: 3 mm of travel against a 2 N/mm spring to a hard stop stands in for the slack between the form and the tie's spreader cone; the far form face and concrete are not modelled. The keyhole is a square with 45 degree shoulders; the flanges are stepped. The wedge is hand-set against 6 N of tie load (a push of about 5 N); the hammer tap that locks it on site is not part of the task. Tie tension is not capped.
